source.title: Searching for Efficient Linear Layers over a Continuous Space of Structured Matrices
source.authors: Andres Potapczynski; Shi-Kai Qiu; Marc Finzi; C. Ferri; Zixi Chen; Micah Goldblum; C. Bruss; Christopher De Sa; Andrew Gordon Wilson

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss against training compute for language models with structured linear layers and compares scaling behavior across structures and settings. This is a conceptual test of compute-related scaling claims, not an explicit reproduction of the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports compute-optimal loss curves for structured layers, including power-law behavior and settings where the curves become less power-law-like. It does not test parameter/token allocation laws or explicitly validate predictions from small-run fits on much larger runs. Its MoE compute-multiplier comparisons and the 17% attention-head efficiency result do not measure power-law form or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits compute-optimal frontiers for GPT-2 with structured (Einsum) linear layers in place of dense ones. It reports that loss follows L = L∞ + bC^-a over roughly 1e14–1e17 FLOPs, and that curves bend in the standard-vocabulary, 512-context setting. This is a new setting (structured layers) with results on the power-law form (V1) and on setup-dependent curvature (V7). The structure comparisons (ω, ψ, ν) measure how layer structure shifts scaling, which no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add that the authors find no existing structure significantly beats dense under compute-optimal training. Also add that BTT-MoE gives a compute multiplier of about 5.3× (E=16), against 4.1× for standard MoE.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GPT-2 with structured linear layers and a reduced-vocabulary OpenWebText setup, comparing compute-optimal curves across structures. It also tests pixel modeling and synthetic regression; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token scaling or prediction protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: The results differ with structure properties ω, ψ, and ν. In the standard 50,257-token vocabulary and sequence-length-512 setting, curves show curvature and ν > 0 structures seem to perform better than ν = 0; the authors suggest vocabulary and context length contribute to these changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing dense layers with structured Einsums changes compute-optimal scaling. More parameter sharing (ω>0) and lower rank (ψ<1) give worse scaling. Among full-rank, no-sharing structures, compute intensity ν has negligible effect, though ν>0 helped in the standard-vocabulary setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal scaling of linear-layer structures is governed mainly by parameters per FLOP and rank, not by density.

record.problems: The main GPT-2 setup reduces the vocabulary to 96 symbols and tests models from 120k to 76M parameters; the standard-vocabulary, longer-context experiment is reported as showing curvature at the tested small scales. The text gives qualitative scaling comparisons but no fitted exponents or direct test of small-run extrapolation to much larger runs. The reported compute-multiplier uncertainty does not quantify uncertainty in the scaling-law fits.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. MoE compute-multiplier comparisons and the attention-head efficiency result are not rows because they report efficiency gains, not the power-law form, extrapolation accuracy, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

untested.parts: Power laws in parameters and tokens separately, with the other not a bottleneck. Only the compute-optimal frontier over about 3 orders of compute, up to 76M parameters, is tested.
No small-run fit is checked against much larger runs. The authors only assert that rates 'can be estimated from small-scale experiments'.
Optimal parameter and token counts versus compute are not reported.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not tested.
Power-law form in pixel modeling and MLP regression is not stated in the text (figure only). Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
Parameter counting, schedule and fitting-method effects on exponents or the compute-optimal split are not tested.

missing.what: Whether the CIFAR-5M and synthetic MLP compute-optimal frontiers follow a power law. Shown only graphically, after subtracting an irreducible loss of 3.25 for CIFAR-5M.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3: a new setting (structured layers), not the original method. V5 gets no verdict because the text never states power-law form for the other modalities. Scales are small (≤76M parameters; ≤GPT-2 Small in the appendix).

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss as a function of compute in selected compute-optimal settings. It does not independently test scaling in parameters or tokens with the other quantities non-bottlenecking, and it does not establish the claimed range of several orders for those separate axes.
No explicit small-run fit is evaluated against the loss of held-out, orders-of-magnitude-larger runs.
The paper compares compute-optimal performance across layer structures, but does not test how the loss-minimising parameter and token counts each vary with compute.
It compares structured linear operators, not the effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests autoregressive pixel modeling and synthetic MLP regression. It does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance or prediction from pretraining loss is evaluated.

Shows setup-related curvature and a change in the effect of compute intensity. It does not compare parameter-counting conventions, data choices, fitting methods, or compute-optimal parameter/token split exponents.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal held-out loss curves for Einsum structures replacing dense layers.

conditions.value: various Einsums, including low-rank, Tensor-Train, BTT, and generic Einsums

rows.value: The loss follows L = L∞ + bC^-a, with possibly different constants a and b; the paper reports subtracting estimated L∞ = 0.75 for Figure 3.
rows.note: The authors state that the different structures can reach arbitrarily low reducible loss at different rates. The figure presents the curves; no fitted exponents are reported in the text.
rows.check: Correct link. Baseline is the fitted form; the value is stated in text only, with no exponents. Compute range is about 1e14–1e17 FLOPs, read from Figure 3.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.1–4.2; Figure 3 caption. Section 4.2 reports L = L∞ + bC^-a and subtracts estimated L∞ = 0.75.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal loss scaling across Einsums with differing parameter-sharing exponent ω.
rows.value: Larger ω values lead to significantly worse scaling laws.
rows.note: The result distinguishes relative scaling among structures; it does not provide numerical exponents.
rows.check: Compares scaling across parameter-sharing levels ω. It does not test whether loss follows a power law, so it does not bear on V1. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal loss scaling across structures without parameter sharing and with differing rank exponent ψ.
rows.value: Structures with ψ < 1 have worse scaling laws; smaller ψ is associated with a more severe information bottleneck.
rows.note: The paper reports a qualitative comparison among structures, not a fitted power-law exponent for each.
rows.check: Compares structures by rank exponent ψ. This is a structure effect on scaling, not a test of the power-law form. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal loss scaling across full-rank, no-parameter-sharing structures with differing compute intensity ν.
rows.value: Structures with different ν have almost indistinguishable scaling laws compared with each other and dense matrices.
rows.note: The authors characterize variation in ν as having minimal effect in this tested subspace.
rows.check: ν has negligible effect among full-rank BTTs. This concerns structured-matrix type, not depth or width at fixed parameter count (V4), and not the power-law form (V1). Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: transformers
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal loss scaling for Einsum structures replacing dense layers.
rows.value: The authors report qualitatively the same effects as in the GPT-2 experiments: ω and ψ have the largest impact, while varying ν yields only slight variations.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative generalization of the scaling-law findings; no exponents are stated.
rows.check: The text's 'same results' refers to ω/ψ/ν effects, not to a power-law fit for pixel modeling. Power-law form is visible only in Figure 5, with an irreducible loss of 3.25 subtracted. Most Einsums beat dense at small scales.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal loss scaling for Einsum structures replacing dense layers.

conditions.value: synthetic data generated by a large randomly initialized MLP

rows.value: The authors report qualitatively the same effects as in the GPT-2 experiments.
rows.note: This is a synthetic regression regime, not language-model pretraining; numerical exponents are not stated.
rows.check: Synthetic MLP regression with raw MSE. The text reports only that the ω/ψ/ν effects match GPT-2; power-law form is not stated.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss scaling for Einsum structures in the standard-vocabulary, longer-context GPT-2 setting.
rows.value: The curves are less power-law-like and show curvature on a log-log scale at the tested small scales.
rows.note: The authors attribute this result as a belief to increased context length and vocabulary, which may cause finite-size effects.
rows.check: For V1 the curves are only partially power-law (curvature). For V7 the row shows the bending the version describes. The authors attribute it to vocabulary and context length at small scale.

source_check.correct: State partial for V1; observed for V7. The reported curvature qualifies the power-law claim and directly exhibits the bending described by V7.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix D.1, especially the paragraph comparing Figures 9 and 4; Figure 9 caption.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state fits V1 but understates the observed V7 effect.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss scaling for structures with differing compute intensity in the standard-vocabulary, longer-context setting.

conditions.value: BTT with ν > 0 compared with ν = 0

rows.value: BTT with ν > 0 seems to perform better than ν = 0; the authors suggest increased compute intensity may shift more compute from the language-modeling head to transformer blocks at small scales.
rows.note: The authors present the explanation as a belief, not a measured causal account.
rows.check: Relative ranking of ν>0 vs ν=0 BTT structures. It is not a measure of power-law form, allocation or fit choice. Moved to fits_no_version.
